Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the parabola shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(-1,2),$ and passes through the point $(1,4).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(-1,2),$ and so we have

$$
x+1=2pt,\,y-2=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(1,4),$ we can substitute $x=1$ and $y=4$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}2=2pt \\ 2=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =2pt \\ 1 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{1}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =p{(\frac{1}{p})}^{2} \\ 2 & =p\cdot \frac{1}{{p}^{2}} \\ 2 & =\frac{1}{p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+1=2(\frac{1}{2})t,\,y-2=(\frac{1}{2}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+1=t,\,y-2=\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}.
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(1,3)$ and which passes through the point $(-1,4)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(1,3),$ and so we have

$$
x-1=2pt,\,y-3=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(-1,4),$ we can substitute $x=-1$ and $y=4$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}-2=2pt \\ 1=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{1}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =p{(-\frac{1}{p})}^{2} \\ 1 & =p\cdot \frac{1}{{p}^{2}} \\ 1 & =\frac{1}{p} \\ p & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-1=2(1)t,\,y-3=(1){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-1=2t,\,y-3={t}^{2}.

questions.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation $(y-3)^{2}=-12(x-5)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(5,3).$ So we have

$$
x-5=p{t}^{2},\,y-3=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =-12(x-5) \\ 4p(x-5) & =-12(x-5) \\ 4p & =-12 \\ p & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-5=(-3){t}^{2},\,y-3=2(-3)t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-5=-3{t}^{2},\,y-3=-6t.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following parametric equation of the parabola 

$$
x-3=-{t}^{2},\,y+4=-2t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

The Cartesian equation of this parabola is

$(y\,+$
{{field-1}}$)^{2}=$
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =-(x-3),\,t=-\frac{y+4}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(-\frac{y+4}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(y+4)^{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=-(x-3)$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(y+4)^{2}}{4} & =-(x-3) \\ (y+4)^{2} & =-4(x-3) \\ {(y+4)}^{2} & =-4(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the parabola defined by the parametric equations

$$
x-4=-2{t}^{2},\,y-1=-4t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =-\frac{x-4}{2},\,t=-\frac{y-1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(-\frac{y-1}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=-\frac{x-4}{2}$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{16} & =-\frac{x-4}{2} \\ (y-1)^{2} & =16\cdot (-\frac{x-4}{2}) \\ (y-1)^{2} & =-8(x-4).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the parabola defined by the parametric equations

$$
x-6=3t,\,y-3=\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2},\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}t & =\frac{x-6}{3},\,{t}^{2}=\frac{2(y-3)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(\frac{x-6}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(x-6)^{2}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=\frac{2(y-3)}{3}$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-6)^{2}}{9} & =\frac{2(y-3)}{3} \\ (x-6)^{2} & =9\cdot (\frac{2(y-3)}{3}) \\ (x-6)^{2} & =6(y-3).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
What set of parametric equations, defined for $t\in(-\infty, \infty),$ generates the parabola shown below?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14041015/assets/1a75a5242f3636efac8def7fc62458e1c1c6972ca79a1ab6fd73af47be622a7a.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(-4,5),$ and passes through the point $(-2,3).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x - h = 2pt, \qquad y - k = pt^2,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k) = (-4,5),$ and so we have

$$
x + 4 = 2pt, \qquad y - 5 = pt^2.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(-2, 3),$ we can substitute $x=-2$ and $y=3$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}2=2pt \\ -2=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =2pt \\ 1 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{1}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =p{(\frac{1}{p})}^{2} \\ -2 & =\frac{1}{p} \\ p & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x + 4 = 2\left(-\dfrac12\right)t, \qquad y - 5 = \left(-\dfrac12\right)t^2 ,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x + 4 = -t, \qquad y - 5 = -\dfrac12t^2 .
$$

The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x - h = pt^2, \qquad y - k = 2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k) = (-3,2),$ and so we have

$$
x+3 = pt^2, \qquad y-2 = 2pt.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(1,0),$ we can substitute $x=1$ and $y=0$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}4=p{t}^{2} \\ -2=2pt.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the second equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{1}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the first equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =p{(-\frac{1}{p})}^{2} \\ 4 & =p\cdot \frac{1}{{p}^{2}} \\ 4 & =\frac{1}{p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+3 = \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)t^2, \qquad y -2 = 2\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)t ,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+3 = \dfrac{1}{4}t^2, \qquad y -2= \dfrac{1}{2}t .
$$

Squaring both sides of the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(-\frac{y+1}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation $t^2 = -\dfrac{x-1}{2}$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{16} & =-\frac{x-1}{2} \\ (y+1)^{2} & =16\cdot (-\frac{x-1}{2}) \\ (y+1)^{2} & =-8(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$
